newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE cocoa ends lower, July sits on 1,000 support.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE cocoa ends lower, July sits on 1,000 support.

text.p: LIFFE cocoa futures closed lower on Tuesday, with July perched on psychological support at 1,000 stg per tonne after slipping to a one-week low earlier in the session.
July ended down 16 stg to 1,000 stg per tonne and September shed 16 to 1,017. Overall volume stood at a modest 5,372 lots.

July started slightly weaker, in line with losses made overnight in New York. Further pressure came from light, outright fund sales, which helped July dip below psychological support at 1,000 near midday.
But most of the volume came from spreads. In the morning, traders said a large, European firm traded 150 to 200 July/September near 18 and 19 stg. The spread closed at 17 stg.

In the afternoon, 750 May/September contracts were said to have been crossed at 25 stg, traders said. September 1998 volume tallied 1,190 contracts, second only to July, which garnered 1,471 trades. All other months traded fewer than 1,000 lots.
Though July fell as low as 997 during the afternoon, it showed some resilience by struggling back toward 1,000 to close off its low.
Some traders expected further price erosion after July broke 1,000, but most expected the contract to hold strong support at the April 9 low of 980 to keep cocoa prices trapped in a range.
July cocoa has held between the April 2 high of 1,065 and 980 for more than a month, and traders saw little impetus for cocoa to break out in either direction any time soon.
They said activity has been lackluster in both directions, reflecting the market's lack of conviction either way.

Industry sources in Abidjan pegged total declared arrivals for the Ivory Coast's 1996/97 (Oct-Sept) cocoa crop at 1.015 million tonnes by May 4, compared with just under 1.045 million by April 30 last year.
Private crop analysts in Abidjan told Reuters they expected a mid-crop between 160,000 to 180,000 tonnes, depending on rains into June.
But the news did little to shake cocoa from its doldrums. Traders said the market had already discounted a large Ivorian crop close to last year's bumper harvest.
